title: The Shah Bano Case
hook: After forty-three years of marriage, a woman found herself divorced and without support.

citations.primary: Mohd. Ahmed Khan v. Shah Bano Begum, (1985) 2 SCC 556, AIR 1985 SC 945

status.explain: Section 125 CrPC applicability to Muslim women was modified by the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act 1986, and later constitutionally harmonized in Danial Latifi (2001).

chain.event: Supreme Court holds Section 125 CrPC applies universally to divorced Muslim women.
Parliament passes Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act 1986.
Danial Latifi v. UOI upholds 1986 Act by interpreting reasonable and fair provision to cover entire life.
Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act criminalizes instant Triple Talaq.

statuteMap.note: Secular provision for maintenance of wives, children, and parents.
Cancellation of maintenance upon payment of customary dues on divorce.

doctrines: Mahr vs. Dues Payable on Divorce

episodes.title: A MARRIAGE OF FORTY-THREE YEARS ENDED IN A MAGISTRATE'S COURT.

blocks.text: Mohd Ahmed Khan, an advocate by profession, married Shah Bano Begum in 1932. Three sons and two daughters were born of the marriage. In 1975, Khan drove Shah Bano out of the matrimonial home. In April 1978, she filed a petition before the Judicial Magistrate (First Class), Indore, under Section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, asking for Rs. 500 a month in maintenance — pointing to Khan's professional income, which she put at roughly Rs. 60,000 a year.

LEGAL ANALYSIS: This episode establishes the factual foundation — marital duration, the husband's declared income, and the petition's statutory basis. It sets up "wife" as the term whose scope will become the case's central question.

student.ratio: Section 125 CrPC applies to a divorced Muslim wife unable to maintain herself, irrespective of personal law, because Mahr is not a sum 'payable on divorce' under Section 127(3)(b) CrPC.

blocks.text: TRIAL PROPOSITION: Establishes the marriage's duration and the husband's declared income — relevant to quantum of maintenance, not to the entitlement question the appeal actually turned on.

howToUse: HOW TO CITE THIS PRECEDENT (FOR COUNSEL): No holding-level proposition in this episode — foundational facts only. Do not cite this passage as authority; cite Episodes 5, 7, and 8 for the operative holdings.
howToDistinguish: HOW OPPOSING COUNSEL WILL DISTINGUISH: A case involving a shorter marriage, or a husband's undisclosed/disputed income, sits on different footing for quantum purposes — though not for the entitlement question this case actually decides.

episodes.endHook: How did the next phase unfold? Continue to Episode 2 ↓

episodes.title: THE PEOPLE BEHIND THE PETITION.

blocks.text:
PERSONA 01 — APPELLANT (HUSBAND)
Mohd Ahmed Khan
Advocate by profession
Married to Shah Bano for over four decades before the dispute reached court. Argued that his obligations under Muslim personal law had already been discharged.

PERSONA 02 — RESPONDENT (WIFE)
Shah Bano Begum
Petitioner for maintenance
Filed for maintenance under Section 125 CrPC after being driven from the matrimonial home in 1975.

PERSONA 03 — INTERVENER
All India Muslim Personal Law Board
Intervened in support of Khan's position on the scope of Muslim personal law.

PERSONA 04 — INTERVENER
Begum Temur Jehan
Social worker
Intervened in support of the counsel appearing for Shah Bano.

LEGAL ANALYSIS: Note the interveners. The All India Muslim Personal Law Board's participation shows this was never a private dispute between two people alone — a religious body sought to shape the outcome, signalling the case's stakes beyond its two named parties.

student.ratio: Section 125 CrPC applies to a divorced Muslim wife unable to maintain herself, irrespective of personal law, because Mahr is not a sum 'payable on divorce' under Section 127(3)(b) CrPC.

blocks.text: TRIAL PROPOSITION: The intervention of the All India Muslim Personal Law Board signals that the case's ratio was argued and tested against the organised institutional position of Muslim personal law, not just one litigant's private defence.

howToUse: HOW TO CITE THIS PRECEDENT (FOR COUNSEL): Not a citable holding — background only.
howToDistinguish: HOW OPPOSING COUNSEL WILL DISTINGUISH: Not applicable to this episode.

episodes.title: A TALAQ ARRIVES WHILE THE PETITION IS STILL PENDING.

blocks.text: While Shah Bano's maintenance petition was pending before the Magistrate, Khan divorced her by an irrevocable talaq on 6 November 1978. His defence shifted accordingly: the divorce, he argued, ended any obligation to maintain her; he had already paid Rs. 200 a month for about two years, and he had deposited Rs. 3,000 in court as dower (Mahr) for her iddat period. In August 1979, the Magistrate ordered him to pay just Rs. 25 a month. Shah Bano moved the Madhya Pradesh High Court in revision — which, in July 1980, raised the amount to Rs. 179.20 a month. Khan appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave.

LEGAL ANALYSIS: The talaq, delivered mid-litigation, is what actually creates the legal question. Before it, Khan was simply a husband who had driven his wife from the home; after it, the question becomes whether "wife" under Section 125's Explanation still reaches a woman who has since been divorced.

student.ratio: Section 125 CrPC applies to a divorced Muslim wife unable to maintain herself, irrespective of personal law, because Mahr is not a sum 'payable on divorce' under Section 127(3)(b) CrPC.

blocks.text: TRIAL PROPOSITION: The talaq's timing — after the petition was filed, before final disposal — did not defeat the claim; the Court tested entitlement against the Explanation (b) definition of "wife," not against the procedural moment of divorce.

pinpoints.proposition: Wife means a wife as defined, irrespective of the religion professed by her or by her husband. Therefore, a divorced Muslim woman so long as she has not married, is a wife for the purpose of section 125.

howToUse: HOW TO CITE THIS PRECEDENT (FOR COUNSEL): PINPOINT: 855A-B; 854B — 'Wife means a wife as defined, irrespective of the religion professed by her or by her husband. Therefore, a divorced Muslim woman so long as she has not married, is a wife for the purpose of section 125.' Cite for: a Muslim woman divorced during or before Section 125 proceedings qualifies as 'wife' under the Explanation, regardless of when in the litigation the divorce occurs.
howToDistinguish: HOW OPPOSING COUNSEL WILL DISTINGUISH: A wife who has remarried after divorce falls outside the Explanation's definition entirely — the judgment's protection is expressly limited to a divorced woman 'so long as she has not remarried.'

episodes.endHook: How did the next phase unfold? Continue to Episode 4 ↓

episodes.kicker: EPISODE 04 · TWO EARLIER RULINGS, ONE DOUBTING BENCH
episodes.title: THE COURT HAD ANSWERED THIS BEFORE. NOW A BENCH WASN'T SURE.

blocks.text: Two earlier three-judge decisions of the Supreme Court — Bai Tahira v. Ali Hussain Fidalli Chothia and Fazlunbi v. K. Khader Vali — had already held that Section 125 applied to Muslims, and that a divorced Muslim wife could claim maintenance under it. But when Khan's appeal reached a Bench of Justices Murtaza Fazal Ali and A. Varadarajan, they doubted those rulings, holding that they might conflict with Section 127(3)(b) of the Code and with Section 2 of the Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act, 1937. On 3 February 1981, they referred the matter to a larger Bench of more than three judges.

LEGAL ANALYSIS: A key procedural point for exams — a smaller Bench that doubts an earlier Bench's ruling cannot simply overrule it. It must refer the matter to a larger Bench, exactly as happened here, which is why this case was ultimately decided by five judges instead of three.

student.ratio: Section 125 CrPC applies to a divorced Muslim wife unable to maintain herself, irrespective of personal law, because Mahr is not a sum 'payable on divorce' under Section 127(3)(b) CrPC.

blocks.text: TRIAL PROPOSITION: A smaller coordinate Bench that doubts an earlier ruling must refer the matter to a larger Bench rather than depart from it directly — the exact mechanism that produced this 5-Judge decision.

howToUse: HOW TO CITE THIS PRECEDENT (FOR COUNSEL): Procedural point; drawn from the Court's own recital of the referral order dated 3 February 1981 (quoted in full in the judgment), not separately pinpointed in the SCR headnote. Cite for: the referral mechanism itself when arguing that a lower or coordinate Bench cannot bypass binding precedent without proper reference.
howToDistinguish: HOW OPPOSING COUNSEL WILL DISTINGUISH: Not applicable — this is settled procedure, not a fact pattern to distinguish.

episodes.endHook: How did the next phase unfold? Continue to Episode 5 ↓

episodes.title: SECTION 125 CrPC VS. THE LIMITS OF IDDAT.

blocks.text:
KHAN'S ARGUMENT
Under Muslim personal law, a husband's liability to maintain his divorced wife ends with the iddat period — regardless of whether she can support herself afterward. Section 127(3)(b) of the Code required the maintenance order to be cancelled once the wife had received 'the whole of the sum... payable on such divorce' under her personal law — and Mahr, Khan argued, was exactly that sum.

SHAH BANO'S ARGUMENT
Section 125 is a secular provision of the criminal code, not a codification of any single religion's law, and covers any wife 'unable to maintain herself,' regardless of her faith. Mahr is not a sum payable 'on divorce' at all — it is payable in consideration of the marriage itself, merely falling due (in its deferred form) on the marriage's dissolution.

LEGAL ANALYSIS: This is the doctrinal core for exam answers — two statutory provisions in tension. Section 125's broad, religion-neutral definition of 'wife' against Section 127(3)(b)'s exception for sums 'payable on divorce' under personal law. Learn exactly what each side argued Mahr actually was.

student.ratio: Section 125 CrPC applies to a divorced Muslim wife unable to maintain herself, irrespective of personal law, because Mahr is not a sum 'payable on divorce' under Section 127(3)(b) CrPC.

blocks.text: TRIAL PROPOSITION: The core statutory-interplay holding — deferred Mahr, though it falls due on dissolution of the marriage, is not a sum 'payable on divorce' within Section 127(3)(b), because it is consideration for the marriage, not for the divorce.

pinpoints.proposition: Divorce may be a convenient or identifiable point of time at which the deferred amount has to be paid by the husband to the wife. But, the payment of the amount is not occasioned by the divorce...

howToUse: HOW TO CITE THIS PRECEDENT (FOR COUNSEL): PINPOINT: 863B-D; 863D-G; 863H — 'Divorce may be a convenient or identifiable point of time at which the deferred amount has to be paid by the husband to the wife. But, the payment of the amount is not occasioned by the divorce...' Cite for: the proposition that a sum merely coinciding with, or contingent on, dissolution of marriage is not automatically a sum 'payable on divorce' under Section 127(3)(b).
howToDistinguish: HOW OPPOSING COUNSEL WILL DISTINGUISH: A personal-law regime where a sum is expressly and solely triggered by the divorce itself (not merely payable in consideration of the marriage and falling due on its end) would sit outside this reasoning — the Court's logic turns specifically on Mahr being marriage-consideration, not divorce-consideration.

episodes.endHook: How did the next phase unfold? Continue to Episode 6 ↓

episodes.title: DOES A SECULAR STATUTE REACH INTO PERSONAL LAW?

blocks.text:
A woman married for more than four decades is left without means to support herself once her husband, exercising a right his personal law gives him, ends the marriage. He says he's already paid what the law requires. She says she still can't maintain herself, and the law owes her more.

Two real positions sat before the Bench:

> Uphold Khan's argument — liability ends at iddat once Mahr is paid; allow the appeal.

> Uphold Shah Bano's claim — Section 125 reaches her regardless of personal law; dismiss the appeal.

LEGAL ANALYSIS: The Court's actual method here is worth noting for exams — it did not simply weigh which law should 'win.' It first asked whether a real conflict between Section 125 and Muslim personal law existed at all, before deciding which would prevail.

student.ratio: Section 125 CrPC applies to a divorced Muslim wife unable to maintain herself, irrespective of personal law, because Mahr is not a sum 'payable on divorce' under Section 127(3)(b) CrPC.

blocks.text: TRIAL PROPOSITION: Framing episode only — no independent holding to cite here.

howToUse: HOW TO CITE THIS PRECEDENT (FOR COUNSEL): Not applicable.
howToDistinguish: HOW OPPOSING COUNSEL WILL DISTINGUISH: Not applicable.

episodes.title: THE APPEAL FAILS. THE MAINTENANCE STANDS.

blocks.text: The five-judge Bench, led by Chief Justice Y.V. Chandrachud, dismissed Khan's appeal and confirmed the Madhya Pradesh High Court's order — directing him to pay Rs. 10,000 in costs to Shah Bano. This was the Supreme Court's final disposition of the matter. The Court held that 'wife' under Section 125's Explanation includes a divorced woman who has not remarried, with no religious qualification attached, and that a Muslim husband's obligation does not automatically end at iddat if his divorced wife remains unable to maintain herself. It further held that Mahr is not a sum 'payable on divorce' under Section 127(3)(b), since it is paid in consideration of the marriage, not the divorce — so Khan's Rs. 3,000 deposit could not cancel the order. The Bench affirmed Bai Tahira and Fazlunbi as correctly decided, with one narrow correction on the Mahr/127(3)(b) point, and pointed to Aiyats 241 and 242 of the Quran as themselves supporting a duty of provision for divorced women.

LEGAL ANALYSIS: Memorize the outcome precisely — appeal dismissed, Madhya Pradesh High Court's order confirmed, Rs. 10,000 costs awarded to the respondent. Note also that Bai Tahira and Fazlunbi were not overruled — they were affirmed, with only a narrow correction on the Mahr/127(3)(b) point.

student.ratio: Section 125 CrPC applies to a divorced Muslim wife unable to maintain herself, irrespective of personal law, because Mahr is not a sum 'payable on divorce' under Section 127(3)(b) CrPC.

blocks.text: TRIAL PROPOSITION: The ratio-bearing holding — Section 125 is secular in character, and a divorced Muslim wife unable to maintain herself is entitled to apply under it, beyond the iddat period. This is the Court's final disposition (Gate 2 confirmed) — safe to cite without a procedural-posture caveat.

pinpoints.proposition: A divorced Muslim wife is, therefore, entitled to apply for maintenance under section 125 of the Code.
Rejection of the argument that a Muslim husband's liability is limited to the iddat period despite the wife's continuing inability to maintain herself.

howToUse: HOW TO CITE THIS PRECEDENT (FOR COUNSEL): PINPOINT: 865H, 866A-C — 'A divorced Muslim wife is, therefore, entitled to apply for maintenance under section 125 of the Code.'

PINPOINT: 838H, 851A-B — rejection of the argument that a Muslim husband's liability is limited to the iddat period despite the wife's continuing inability to maintain herself. Cite for: the core holding on Section 125's applicability to Muslims, and the 'unable to maintain herself' standard displacing any personal-law iddat cap.
howToDistinguish: HOW OPPOSING COUNSEL WILL DISTINGUISH: This holding is expressly conditioned on the wife being 'unable to maintain herself.' Per PINPOINT: 858D-G; 859C-D, a divorced wife shown to be capable of self-maintenance falls back to the personal-law position — liability ceasing at iddat. A respondent with demonstrated means of self-support is materially distinguishable on this fact alone.

episodes.title: SECTION 125 IS SECULAR. IT DOES NOT ASK YOUR RELIGION.

blocks.text:
Section 125 CrPC is a provision of general, secular application that does not yield to personal law. A divorced Muslim wife unable to maintain herself is entitled to maintenance under it, even beyond the iddat period — because Mahr is not a sum 'payable on divorce' within Section 127(3)(b), and because Muslim personal law, on the Court's reading, does not contemplate leaving an indigent divorced wife without support at all.

The Court also placed on record a separate observation — not part of its operative holding — regretting that Article 44 of the Constitution, the directive to secure a Uniform Civil Code, remained unimplemented, and urging the State to act on it.

LEGAL ANALYSIS: This is the case to cite for 'Section 125 CrPC is secular and religion-neutral in application' and for 'Mahr is not a sum payable on divorce under Section 127(3)(b).' Keep the Article 44 / Uniform Civil Code passage separate in your notes — the judgment itself frames it as an 'Observation,' not as part of the operative ratio.

student.ratio: Section 125 CrPC applies to a divorced Muslim wife unable to maintain herself, irrespective of personal law, because Mahr is not a sum 'payable on divorce' under Section 127(3)(b) CrPC.
student.examAngle:
Provisions Involved: CrPC §125 (maintenance of wives, children, parents); CrPC §127(3)(b); §2, Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act, 1937; Article 44, Constitution of India (obiter only)
Precedents Relied On / Affirmed: Bai Tahira v. Ali Hussain Fidalli Chothia [1979] 2 SCR 75; Fazlunbi v. K. Khader Vali [1980] 3 SCR 1127; Jagir Kaur v. Jaswant Singh [1964] 2 SCR 73; Nanak Chand v. Shri Chandra Kishore Agarwala [1970] 1 SCR 565; Hamira Bibi v. Zubaida Bibi 43 IA 294; Syed Sabir Hussain v. Farzand Hasan 65 IA 119

blocks.text: TRIAL PROPOSITION: The general proposition that Section 125 CrPC is religion-neutral, plus a caution on the non-binding Article 44 observation.

pinpoints.proposition: Section 125 is truly secular in character... Whether the spouses are Hindus or Muslims, Christians or Parsis, Pagans or Heathens, is wholly irrelevant in the application of these provisions.

howToUse: HOW TO CITE THIS PRECEDENT (FOR COUNSEL): PINPOINT: 834D-E; 855E-G — 'Section 125 is truly secular in character... Whether the spouses are Hindus or Muslims, Christians or Parsis, Pagans or Heathens, is wholly irrelevant in the application of these provisions.' Cite for: the general, religion-neutral character of Section 125 CrPC (now mirrored in Section 144, Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023) in any matter involving maintenance across personal-law lines.
howToDistinguish: HOW OPPOSING COUNSEL WILL DISTINGUISH: The Article 44/Uniform Civil Code passage is expressly headed 'OBSERVATION' in the report and is not part of the operative ratio. A submission that relies on this case for a Uniform Civil Code argument can be met with the objection that the passage is obiter, not binding precedent — the binding holding is confined to Sections 125 and 127(3)(b) CrPC.

vote.question: Does Section 125 CrPC override Muslim Personal Law regarding maintenance of a divorced wife after the Iddat period?
vote.context: The Constitution Bench had to decide if a secular criminal procedural remedy overrides religious personal law when a divorced wife is indigent.

options.label: Personal Law Prevails
options.argument: Maintenance is strictly limited to the Iddat period and Mehr as prescribed by personal law.

options.label: Section 125 Overrides
options.argument: Section 125 CrPC is a secular, universal anti-vagrancy measure applying regardless of religion.

glossary.inThisCase: The period of waiting observed by a Muslim woman following the dissolution of marriage or death of her husband, during which she cannot remarry.
A mandatory payment, in the form of money or possessions paid or promised by the groom to the bride at the time of Islamic marriage.
An instantaneous and irreversible dissolution of marriage pronounced by the husband.

flashcards.q: What was the central question in Mohd. Ahmed Khan v. Shah Bano Begum (1985)?
flashcards.a: Whether Section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure applies to a divorced Muslim woman unable to maintain herself, even beyond the iddat period and despite payment of Mahr.

flashcards.q: What was the Supreme Court's holding on Section 125 CrPC and personal law?
flashcards.a: Section 125 CrPC is a secular provision of general application designed to prevent vagrancy and applies to all citizens irrespective of religion.

flashcards.q: Why did the Court hold Mahr does not trigger Section 127(3)(b) CrPC?
flashcards.a: Mahr is paid in consideration of the marriage, not the divorce. Hence, it is not a sum 'payable on divorce' under Section 127(3)(b).

flashcards.q: What was the Bench composition and author of the judgment?
flashcards.a: 5-Judge Constitution Bench headed and authored by Chief Justice Y.V. Chandrachud (with Misra, Desai, Reddy, and Venkataramiah, JJ.).

affectsYou.heading: Why the Shah Bano precedent protects rights today
points: Establishes that economic vulnerability takes precedence over personal law exemptions in criminal maintenance petitions.
Reaffirms the principle that statutory social-welfare legislation applies universally across religious identities in India.
Directly led to the 1986 Act and the Danial Latifi constitutional compromise ensuring long-term financial security for divorced women.

timeline.event: Mohd Ahmed Khan marries Shah Bano Begum.
Khan drives Shah Bano out of the matrimonial home.
Shah Bano files petition under Section 125 CrPC; Khan pronounces irrevocable talaq.
Judicial Magistrate Indore awards Rs. 25 per month.
Madhya Pradesh High Court enhances maintenance to Rs. 179.20 per month.
Supreme Court 2-judge bench refers the matter to a 5-judge Constitution Bench.
Supreme Court dismisses husband's appeal and affirms Section 125's secular application.

subsequentHistory.citation: Danial Latifi v. Union of India (2001) 7 SCC 740
subsequentHistory.summary: Upheld the constitutional validity of the 1986 Muslim Women Act by interpreting Section 3(1)(a) to mean that a reasonable and fair provision must be made within the iddat period for the divorced wife's entire future life, reaffirming the essence of Shah Bano.

subsequentHistory.citation: Shabana Bano v. Imran Khan (2010) 1 SCC 216
subsequentHistory.summary: Reiterated that a divorced Muslim woman is entitled to claim maintenance under Section 125 CrPC as long as she does not remarry, even after expiry of the iddat period.

subsequentHistory.citation: Mohd Abdul Samad v. State of Telangana (2024) 8 SCC 419
subsequentHistory.summary: Reaffirmed that Section 125 CrPC is an independent secular remedy available to divorced Muslim women in addition to the 1986 Act.
